title: Balanced Search Tree From a Sorted Chain
statement:
You get the head of a singly linked list whose values are strictly increasing. Build a binary search tree that holds exactly these values and is height-balanced: at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. Return its root.

Several trees usually qualify, for example when a range has two middle values. Any valid balanced search tree is accepted.

examples.why: 0 is the middle value, so it becomes the root, with two values on each side. [0, -2, 4, -6, null, null, 11] is just as valid.
Two values: either can be the root. [8, 3] is also accepted.
Seven values fill three levels completely. Using the first value as root would give a chain of height 7.

hints: In a balanced search tree, which value should sit at the root?
The middle value: it splits the rest into two halves of nearly equal size, and each half becomes a balanced subtree by the same rule.

Finding the middle of a list is O(n). Instead, build the tree in in-order: recurse on the left half's size first, then take the current list node as the root, then recurse on the right half. The list pointer advances in exactly sorted order.

explain.intuition:
Pick the middle value as the root. The left half has the smaller values and the right half the larger ones, and their sizes differ by at most 1. Repeat on each half and every node ends up balanced. With an array this is easy, because the middle is one index away.

A linked list has no cheap middle. The neat trick is to notice that an in-order walk of the finished tree visits values in sorted order, which is exactly the order of the list. So build the tree in in-order: knowing only the size of a range, first build its left subtree (which consumes the first half of the list), then take the current list node as the root, then build the right subtree. A single pointer moves through the list once.
steps: Count the nodes: n. Keep a pointer cur = head.
Otherwise let leftSize = floor(size / 2) and build the left subtree with build(leftSize).
Create the root from cur.val and advance cur. Then build the right subtree with build(size − leftSize − 1).
pitfalls: Taking the first list node as the root. That builds a chain, the opposite of balanced.
Finding the middle with slow and fast pointers at every level and forgetting to cut the list before the middle. The left half then still runs into the right half.
Using a local copy of the list pointer in the in-order version. The pointer must be shared, so the right subtree continues where the left one stopped.

solutions.title: Copy to an array, split at the middle
solutions.idea: Turn the list into an array so the middle is one index away, then recurse on both halves.

solutions.title: Build in in-order with one list pointer
solutions.idea: In-order visits values in sorted order, the same order as the list. Build the left subtree from a size, take the current node as root, then build the right subtree.

followups: Do it with slow and fast pointers to find each middle. What is the running time, and why?
The input is a sorted array instead. Which version becomes the obvious one?
